chapter_theme: Speech is an excellence in its own right and a source of gain and ruin. Its mastery means fitting the hearer, being unanswerable, being brief when one can and expansive when one must; learning that can't be spoken has no fragrance.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: why speech is indispensable (641-642), what speech is (643), how to speak (644-646), the distinction of those able to speak so (647-648), and the low standing of those who can't (649-650). He reads the whole as addressed to ministers.

641.reading: Having the goodness called goodness of tongue is a good that isn't contained in any other good.
641.nuance: The verse is about the excellence of speech as such; it does not mention ministers. Parimelazhagar draws them in from the chapter's position and also argues that if others need it, ministers need it more.

642.reading: Since gain and ruin both come from it, guard against any lapse in speech.
642.nuance: சோர்வு is a slip, not malice. Parimelazhagar widens the stakes: a minister's lapse falls on all living beings at once.

643.reading: Speech is what is said so that it binds those who hear it and makes even those who have not heard want it.
643.nuance: The second half is the striking one: speech is judged partly by its effect on those not present. Parimelazhagar lists good speech's qualities here as freedom from error, brevity, clarity, sweetness and valuable result.

positions.position: Hearers are allies who accepted him and non-hearers are hostile parties won over. He criticises all others for reading தகையவாய் as 'having worth'.
positions.quote: நட்பாய் ஏற்றுக் கொண்டாரைப் பின் வேறுபடாமல் பிணிக்கும் குணங்களை அவாவி

positions.position: Those are the ones who asked and the ones who did not ask.
positions.quote: வினாவினாரைப் பிணித்துக் கொள்ளுந் தகையவாய், வினாவாதா ரும் விரும்புமாறு

644.reading: Speak with knowledge of what the moment and hearer require, for no virtue or gain goes beyond that.
644.nuance: A surprising claim: fit speech ranks at the top of both virtue and gain. Parimelazhagar explains that the cause stands for the effect.

positions.position: The 'capacities' are differences of rank by birth, learning, conduct, wealth, form and age, and to speak according to them is the virtue.
positions.quote: குடிப்பிறப்பு, கல்வி, ஒழுக்கம், செல்வம், உருவம், பருவம் என்பவற்றான் வரும் தகுதி வேறுபாடுகள்.

positions.position: It's the way of speaking: knowing this avoids slander, empty talk and lying, so it becomes virtue.
positions.quote: புறங்கூறாமையும் பயனில சொல்லாமையும் பொய்கூறா மையும் உளவாம்

positions.position: It means knowing clearly the reason for saying something.

645.reading: Speak your word once you know there is no other word that can defeat it.
645.nuance: சொல் occurs five times, so the verse is a sort of closed argument. Parimelazhagar says winning means excelling in the qualities of speech, which is a broader standard than mere refutation.

646.reading: It is the way of those without blemish in excellence to speak so that others want more and to take the fruit from what others say.
646.nuance: Mastery of speech includes a discipline of hearing. Parimelazhagar adds generosity: a master doesn't scorn others' faulty words, and takes what is useful in them.

647.reading: It's hard for anyone to beat in a contest a person who can speak, doesn't slip, and isn't afraid.
647.nuance: Parimelazhagar's gloss of 'speaking so that it is accepted' is uncomfortable: making people decide 'yes' even where the thing isn't actually in their interest. Eloquence, in that reading, isn't truthful by nature, and the chapter doesn't address this.

648.reading: The world quickly responds if it gets those who can speak in order and sweetly.
648.nuance: பெறின், 'if it gets', implies rarity. Parimelazhagar cites a Sanskrit saying that a true speaker is one in a hundred thousand.

positions.position: தொழில் is what is being said, and the world accepts these matters readily.
தொழில் is work to do: people rush up and ask what they must do.
positions.quote: உலகத்தார் மேவி விரைந்து சென்று செய்யுந் தொழில் யாது என்று கேட்பர்

649.reading: Those who don't know how to say a few faultless words surely long to say many.
649.nuance: Loquacity is explained as a substitute for an ability, not an excess of it. Parimelazhagar takes மன்ற as a firm answer to those who actually admire nonstop speech as eloquence.

650.reading: Those who can't unfold what they've learned so that others understand are like flowers blooming in clusters without scent.
650.nuance: Coming right after 649's praise of few words, this verse praises expansion. Manakkudavar notices this: brevity alone isn't enough, and one must also expand where needed. In the image, learning is already in bloom; what is missing is the part that travels to others.

links.note: 32 says nothing brings more gain than virtue, and 644 uses the same ஊங்கு formula to put apt speech above both virtue and gain. This is either high rhetoric or a real rearrangement. Parimelazhagar makes apt speech a cause of virtue to avoid the clash.

127, in the Virtue book, says guard the tongue or suffer from its errors, and the fear is personal shame. 642 makes the same demand for a public reason, since gain and ruin follow. The same discipline serves different goals.

424 defines wisdom by the same two-part structure: making your speech enter easily and finding the fine meaning in others' words. 646 assigns it to excellence in office, so wisdom and diplomacy are shown to share a form.

source_issues: 641: Manakkudavar's commentary is marked as not aligned in the source.
648: Parimelazhagar's lemma reads செல்லுதல் where the verse has சொல்லுதல்.
650: The verse begins இண்ருழ்த்தும், a typographical error for இணரூழ்த்தும் (commentaries give இணர் ஊழ்த்தும்).
